blocks.html: When we talk, we say whole ideas: “The dog is barking.” “I ate my lunch.” When we write a whole idea, we call it a sentence.
A sentence has two jobs. It tells who or what the idea is about, and it tells what happens.

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.sentence: A frog jumps into the pond.

blocks.cap: Who or what? A frog. What happens? It jumps into the pond.

blocks.html: A sentence tells a whole idea: who or what, and what happens.
A reader can’t ask you what you meant. If you write only “The frog.”, the reader is left waiting: what about the frog? A whole sentence answers both questions, so the reader understands.

blocks.title: Is it a sentence?
blocks.q: “The big red ball.”
steps: Who or what? The big red ball.
What happens? It doesn’t say.
It is only part of an idea, so it is not a sentence yet.
We could finish it: “The big red ball rolls down the hill.”
blocks.a: Not yet. It needs what happens.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: The cat sleeps on the bed.

cards.why: It tells who, but not what happens.
Short, but whole: who (birds) and what happens (sing).
Who ran? It never says.
It tells where, but not who or what happens.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. For each one, ask: who or what? What happens?

blocks.cap: Sort the cards: sentence or not a sentence.

blocks.html: Thinking that a capital letter and a period make a sentence. “The big dog.” has both, but it is still only part of an idea. Check by asking the two questions: who or what? What happens?

For the grown-up. A sentence can be very short (“Birds sing.”) and a long string of words can still be unfinished. Read your child’s writing aloud with them and ask, “What happens?” when a sentence stops too soon. The site’s guides to The Mother Tongue begin the same way, with saying whole thoughts aloud before writing them.

blocks.html: In What Is a Sentence? you learned that a sentence tells who or what, and what happens. The words also need to go in an order that makes sense.
Most telling sentences start with who or what, then tell what happens, then tell more, like where.

head: Who or what
What happens
More
blocks.cap: Three sentences, each in the usual order.

blocks.html: Put the words in an order that makes sense: usually who or what first, then what happens. Read it aloud to check.
In English, the order of words carries meaning. “The dog chased the cat.” and “The cat chased the dog.” use the same words, but they tell different stories. Mixed-up words leave the reader guessing.

blocks.title: Fix the order
blocks.q: The words are mixed up: “sings bird a tree the in”
steps: Who or what? A bird.
What happens? It sings.
Where? In the tree.
Put them together and add a capital and a period.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: The
girl
flies
a
kite.
opts.title: Put the word cards in order.

blocks.cap: Tap two cards to swap them. Then Check.

blocks.html: Writing words in the order you think of them, like “Ball the kicked Sam.” Read your sentence aloud. If it doesn’t sound like talking, move the words around.
For the grown-up. Writing sentences on strips of paper and cutting them into word cards makes a good game. Mix them up and let your child rebuild the sentence, then read it aloud together.

blocks.html: A sentence needs a clear start, so the reader knows a new idea is beginning. We mark the start with a capital letter: a big letter, like T instead of t.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: the sun is hot. we go to the beach.
answer: The sun is hot. We go to the beach.
opts.note: The underlined letters were changed to capitals.

blocks.cap: Two sentences, two capital letters: one at the start of each.

blocks.html: The first word of every sentence begins with a capital letter.
A period shows where one idea stops, and the capital letter right after it shows where the next idea starts. Together they help the reader’s eyes find each sentence.

blocks.title: Two sentences in a row
blocks.q: “We went to the park. we saw a duck.”
steps: Find the period: after “park.”
The next word, “we,” starts a new sentence.
It needs a capital: “We.”
blocks.a: “We went to the park. We saw a duck.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: my dog likes to run. he runs fast.
answer: My dog likes to run. He runs fast.
opts.hint: Tap a word to switch its first letter between small and capital. Then Check.

blocks.cap: Fix the capital letters.

blocks.html: Remembering the capital on the first sentence, then forgetting it on the next ones. After every period, look at the next word: it starts a new sentence.

For the grown-up. Capital letters belong at the start of a sentence, on the word I, and on names. Children sometimes write capitals anywhere they like the look of them; gently point back to these three places.

blocks.html: Some sentences tell something: “The cat sleeps on the bed.” “I have a red bike.” They are called telling sentences, and they are the kind we write most.
A telling sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a period (.), a small dot that means “this idea is done.”

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.sentence: The cat sleeps on the bed.

blocks.cap: A telling sentence about the picture, with a period at the end.

blocks.html: A telling sentence tells something. It ends with a period.
When you read aloud, your voice drops and you pause at a period. The period tells the reader to do the same: stop, then start the next idea.

blocks.title: Where do the periods go?
blocks.q: “We went to the lake the water was cold”
steps: Read it aloud and listen for where one idea stops.
The first idea: “We went to the lake.”
The second idea: “The water was cold.”
Put a period after each, and a capital at the start of the second.
blocks.a: “We went to the lake. The water was cold.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: Sam has a kite the kite is red
answer: Sam has a kite. The kite is red.

blocks.cap: Tap a space to add a period. Tap a word to give it a capital. Then Check.

blocks.html: Putting a period at the end of every line on the page, even in the middle of an idea. A period goes where the idea ends, wherever that is on the line.
For the grown-up. Reading the writing aloud together is the best check: wherever your voice stops, there should be a period.

blocks.html: Some sentences ask something: “Where is my hat?” “Can we go to the park?” Someone could answer them. They are called asking sentences, or questions.
An asking sentence ends with a question mark (?) instead of a period.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: I know where the cat is
cards.why: It has the word where, but it tells something. Nobody needs to answer it.

cards.text: Mom asked who was at the door
cards.why: It tells what Mom asked. It is a telling sentence.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Could someone answer it?

blocks.cap: Telling or asking? The end marks are missing on purpose.

blocks.html: An asking sentence asks something. It ends with a question mark.
When we ask aloud, our voice often goes up at the end. A reader can’t hear your voice, so the question mark shows that you are asking and waiting for an answer.

blocks.title: Asking or telling?
blocks.q: “I wonder what is in the box”
steps: It has the word what in it.
But it tells what you are wondering. Nobody has to answer.
So it is a telling sentence, and it ends with a period.
blocks.a: “I wonder what is in the box.”

blocks.title: Add the end mark
blocks.q: “What is in the box”
steps: This one asks. Someone could answer, “A puppy!”
So it ends with a question mark.

blocks.html: Seeing a question word like where, who or what and adding a question mark. Words like these can sit inside a telling sentence too: “I know where the ball is.” Ask: does the sentence ask something?
For the grown-up. Play “ask it, tell it”: you say a telling sentence (“The dog is hungry.”) and your child turns it into a question (“Is the dog hungry?”), then writes both with the right marks.

blocks.html: Some sentences show strong feeling: surprise, joy, fear or excitement. “Wow, the cake is huge!” “Look out!” They are called exclamations.
An exclamation ends with an exclamation point (!), a line with a dot under it.

blocks.name: wr-picture
blocks.cap: Say it the way you would on the first snowy morning.

blocks.html: An exclamation shows strong feeling. It ends with one exclamation point.
An exclamation point tells the reader how the words would sound: loud, happy, scared or surprised. If every sentence had one, none of them would stand out, so we save it for real feeling.

blocks.title: What kind of sentence?
blocks.q: “What a big fish”
steps: It starts with What, like many questions.
But it doesn’t ask anything. Nobody answers it.
It shows surprise, so it is an exclamation.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: The soup is in the pot

cards.why: It starts with What but shows surprise. Nobody answers it.

cards.text: Look out, a bee is coming
cards.why: It is a warning, said loud and fast.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud with feeling. Which mark does it need?

blocks.cap: Three kinds of sentences, three end marks.

blocks.html: Putting exclamation points on every sentence, or three in a row (!!!). Use one, and only when the feeling is strong.

For the grown-up. Some sentences can be telling or exclaiming depending on how they are said (“We won the game.” or “We won the game!”). Both can be right; ask your child how the person in the story feels.

blocks.html: You know telling sentences. Some sentences do a different job: they tell someone to do something. “Please shut the door.” “Feed the fish.” We call them bossy sentences, or commands.
A command often starts with the action word: Feed the fish. Put on your coat. Adding please makes it kind.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: It tells someone to do something. The one who sits is the person you are talking to.
It tells what Grandpa does. Nobody is being told to do anything.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Is someone being told to do something?

blocks.cap: Telling or bossy? Sort the cards.

blocks.html: A command tells someone to do something. It usually ends with a period.
When you say “Feed the fish” to your brother, you don’t say his name first. He knows you mean him. A command works the same way on paper: the person reading or listening is the one who does it.

blocks.title: Is it a sentence?
blocks.q: “Close the gate.”
steps: Who is told to close the gate? The person you are talking to.
What happens? Close the gate.
It is a whole idea, so yes, it is a sentence: a command.
blocks.a: Yes. It is a command, and it ends with a period.

blocks.html: Thinking “Close the gate.” is not a sentence because nobody is named. In a command, the one who does it is you, the person spoken to. It is as if the sentence said “You, close the gate.”

For the grown-up. A command said with strong feeling, like a warning, can end with an exclamation point: “Look out!” Most everyday commands end with a period. Play “Teddy says”: take turns giving each other commands, then write two of them down.

blocks.html: You have learned four kinds of sentences: telling, asking, exclamations and commands. Each one needs an end mark. Here is how to choose.

head: The sentence…
End mark
Example
rows: The cake is in the oven.
blocks.cap: Read the whole sentence, then choose.

blocks.html: Read the whole sentence. Does it tell, ask or show strong feeling? Then choose the period, question mark or exclamation point.
End marks tell the reader how to say a sentence: calm, asking, or with feeling. The same words can mean different things: “You ate the cake.” and “You ate the cake?” and “You ate the cake!”

blocks.title: Don’t stop at the first word
blocks.q: “What a big cake”
steps: It starts with What, like many questions.
But nobody can answer it. It shows surprise.
So it ends with an exclamation point.

blocks.title: A question word inside
blocks.q: “I know where the spoon is”
steps: It has the word where in it.
But it tells what I know. It does not ask.
So it ends with a period.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: Look at the cake What a big cake Did you bake it
answer: Look at the cake. What a big cake! Did you bake it?
Look at the cake! What a big cake! Did you bake it?

blocks.cap: Tap each space where a sentence ends and choose its mark. Then Check.

blocks.html: Choosing the mark from the first word alone. “What a big cake!” starts like a question, but it shows surprise. “I know where it is.” has a question word, but it tells. Read to the end before you choose.

For the grown-up. Read sentences aloud in three voices: calm, asking and excited. Children hear the difference before they can explain it. A command like “Look at the cake” can take a period or, said with excitement, an exclamation point.

blocks.html: Every sentence tells who or what. The word that names who or what is a noun, a naming word.
A noun names a person (teacher, Grandma), a place (park, kitchen), an animal (puppy, frog) or a thing (cup, kite).

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: A city is a place. Places are nouns too.

opts.readme: Read each word aloud. Is it a person, a place, an animal or a thing?

blocks.cap: Every card is a noun. Sort them into four kinds.

blocks.html: A noun names a person, a place, an animal or a thing.
Nouns are the names we give to everything around us. Without them a reader would not know who or what a sentence is about: “The ___ ate the ___.”

blocks.title: Find the nouns
blocks.q: “The baker makes bread in the kitchen.”
steps: Baker names a person: a noun.
Bread names a thing: a noun.
Kitchen names a place: a noun.
Makes tells an action, so it is not a noun.

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: The|- teacher|n read|v a|- story|n in|- the|- library|n.

blocks.cap: Tap every noun, then Check.

blocks.html: Counting only things you can touch. Teacher and kitchen are nouns too: a person and a place. Ask: does this word name a person, a place, an animal or a thing?

For the grown-up. Play “I spy a noun” around the house: take turns naming a person, a place, an animal and a thing you can see. Harvey’s grammar, in the site’s teaching guides, starts with names of things the same way.

blocks.html: A noun can name one thing or more than one. One cat, two cats. To mean more than one, most nouns add -s.
Nouns that end in s, x, sh, ch or z add -es: box, boxes; dish, dishes; bus, buses. Say them aloud: the -es adds an extra beat.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: How does each noun show more than one?

blocks.html: Add -s to most nouns. Add -es after s, x, sh, ch and z. A few nouns change in their own way.
Try saying “boxs.” Your mouth wants to add a beat: box-es. The spelling -es matches that extra beat, so readers say the word the way we do.

blocks.title: One fox, two…
blocks.q: What is more than one fox?
steps: Fox ends in x.
Nouns that end in x add -es.
Say it: fox-es, two beats.

blocks.title: A noun that changes
blocks.q: What is more than one mouse?
steps: Mouses doesn’t sound right.
Mouse changes in its own way.
One mouse, two mice.

blocks.html: Writing boxs and dishs, or mouses and foots. Say the word aloud: does it need an extra beat? Is it one of the nouns that change in their own way, like mice, feet, teeth and children?
For the grown-up. Some nouns stay the same for one and many: one sheep, two sheep; one deer, three deer. Rules for words that end in y (pony, ponies) come later, in the Grammar course.

blocks.html: A noun names who or what. A verb tells what they do. In “The dog digs,” dog is the noun and digs is the verb.

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.sentence: The girl flies a kite. The dog runs.

blocks.cap: Flies and runs are verbs: they tell what the girl and the dog do.

blocks.html: A verb tells what someone or something does.
A sentence needs something to happen. The verb is the word that makes it happen. Take it away and the sentence stops: “The dog ___ in the yard.”

blocks.title: Find the verb
blocks.q: “Grandma bakes a cake.”
steps: Who is it about? Grandma.
What does she do? She bakes.
So bakes is the verb.

blocks.title: A quiet verb
blocks.q: “The baby sleeps in her crib.”
steps: Who is it about? The baby.
What does she do? She sleeps.
Sleeping is not a big movement, but it is still something the baby does.

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: The|- cat|n stretches|v, yawns|v and|- naps|v.

blocks.cap: Tap every verb, then Check.

blocks.html: Picking the person or thing instead of the action, or missing quiet verbs. Sleep, wish, know, think and listen are verbs too. Ask: what does this person or thing do?
For the grown-up. Act it out: one of you does an action and the other names the verb. Then try quiet ones together, like think, wait and listen.

blocks.html: A verb tells what happens. It also tells when: yesterday, today or tomorrow.

head: Yesterday (past)
Every day (present)
Tomorrow (future)
blocks.cap: Most verbs add -ed for the past. Will goes before the verb for the future.

blocks.name: wr-tense
blocks.cap: Choose past, present or future and watch the verb change.

blocks.html: Verbs show when: yesterday I walked, today I walk, tomorrow I will walk.
The verb lets a reader know if something already happened, happens now, or hasn’t happened yet. “I walked to school” is a memory; “I will walk to school” is a plan.

blocks.title: Pick the time
blocks.q: “Tomorrow we ___ apples.” (pick)
steps: Tomorrow means later: the future.
For the future, put will before the verb.

blocks.title: A verb that changes its own way
blocks.q: “Yesterday I ___ to the park.” (run)
steps: Yesterday means the past.
Run does not add -ed. Runned is not a word in writing.
Its past form is ran.

blocks.html: Adding -ed to every verb: runned, goed, eated. Some verbs change in their own way: ran, went, ate, saw, came. If a past word sounds odd, say it aloud and listen.

For the grown-up. Young children often say “goed” because they have learned the -ed rule, which is a good sign. Gently say the sentence back the standard way (“Yes, you went to the park!”). When your child writes a story, check that it stays in one time.

blocks.html: Is, are, was and were are small but busy verbs. Which one to use depends on the noun: one, or more than one. It also depends on the time.

head: One (and he, she, it)
More than one (and we, they, you)
blocks.cap: With you, always use are and were.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Mia and Leo are two people: more than one.
You always goes with are.
Bus ends in s, but it means one bus.

blocks.cap: Is or are? Sort the sentences.

blocks.html: One: is, was. More than one, and you: are, were. Other verbs match too: he hops, we hop.
The verb and its noun work as a team. When the verb matches, the reader can tell at once whether you mean one or many.

blocks.title: Two people
blocks.q: “Yesterday we ___ late.” (was or were)
steps: We means more than one.
Yesterday means the past.
More than one, in the past: were.

blocks.html: Many people say “we was” or “they is” when they talk, and that is fine at home. Written standard English uses we were and they are, so in writing, check: one or more than one?
For the grown-up. This is about the written standard, not about which way of talking is better. You might say, “In books, it’s written we were.” With I, use am and was: I am, I was.

blocks.html: Read this: “Grandma baked bread. Grandma gave Grandma’s bread to Grandma’s friend.” Too many Grandmas! Words like she and her can take the place of a noun. They are called pronouns.

head: Instead of…
say…
blocks.cap: Pronouns that can start a sentence. I is one too.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which pronoun can take each one’s place?

blocks.html: A pronoun takes the place of a noun: I, he, she, it, we, they.
Once the reader knows who you mean, saying the name again and again sounds bumpy. A pronoun points back to the noun, so the writing flows.

blocks.title: Swap the noun
blocks.q: “The ducks are hungry. ___ swim to the bread.”
steps: The ducks means more than one.
More than one: they.

blocks.title: Two people doing something
blocks.q: Which is written in standard English: “Me and him played tag.” or “He and I played tag.”?
steps: Try each person alone: “He played tag.” “I played tag.”
“Me played tag” does not sound right in writing.
So write: “He and I played tag.”

blocks.html: Starting a sentence with “Me and him…”. Many people say it, but in writing the ones who do the action are I, he, she, we and they. Try each person alone to check, and name yourself last.
For the grown-up. The test of trying each person alone works for any pair: “Mom and I” → “Mom went” and “I went.” Pronouns like me and him come in the Usage and Mechanics course.

blocks.html: A noun names a thing. A describing word tells more about it: what color, what size, what shape, how many, or what it is like. Describing words are called adjectives.
“A frog sat on a log.” is fine. “A tiny green frog sat on a big log.” helps the reader see it.

blocks.name: wr-tag

opts.text: A|- tiny|adj green|adj frog|n sat|v on|- a|- big|adj log|n.

blocks.cap: Tap every describing word, then Check.

blocks.html: An adjective describes a noun: what color, what size, what shape, how many, or what it is like.
Your reader can’t see what you saw. A few good describing words put the picture in the reader’s mind: not just a dog, but a muddy dog.

blocks.title: Which word describes?
blocks.q: “Dad wore a funny hat.”
steps: Find the nouns: Dad, hat.
What kind of hat? A funny hat.
So funny is the describing word, and it tells about the hat.

blocks.title: How many is describing too
blocks.q: “Mia has three fish.”
steps: How many fish? Three.
Three tells about the fish, so it is a describing word.

blocks.html: Picking the noun instead of the word that describes it, or using the same tired words (nice, good, big) every time. Ask “what kind?” and try a sharper word: not a good cake, a sweet, sticky cake.
For the grown-up. Hold up an object, like an apple or a sock, and take turns saying a describing word for it until you run out. Then use the best two in a sentence.

blocks.html: Some describing words tell how something looks. Good writers use all five senses: how things look, sound, smell, taste and feel.

head: Sense
Words
blocks.cap: Some words fit more than one sense: soup can smell sweet and taste sweet.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which sense does each word go with?

blocks.html: Sense words tell how something looks, sounds, smells, tastes and feels.
When you remember a day at the beach, you remember more than the sight: the crashing waves, the salty air, the hot sand. Sense words let a reader feel they were there too.

blocks.title: Add a sense
blocks.q: Make this better with a sense word for taste: “The lemon was yellow.”
steps: Yellow tells how it looks.
How does a lemon taste? Sour.
Add it: “The yellow lemon was sour.”

blocks.html: Describing only how things look. Before you write, close your eyes and ask: What do I hear? What do I smell? What does it feel like?
For the grown-up. At snack time, ask one question for each sense: How does it look? Sound when you bite it? Smell? Taste? Feel? Write down the best words together.

blocks.html: A short sentence can grow. Add describing words and words that tell where or when, and a plain sentence becomes a picture.

blocks.name: wr-revise

opts.after: The little brown dog ran to the lake.
opts.title: A sentence that grew

blocks.cap: Two describing words and a where phrase were added.

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.sentence: The busy duck swims on the pond in the sunshine.

blocks.cap: The duck swims. → The busy duck swims on the pond in the sunshine.

blocks.html: To make a sentence grow, add what kind (describing words), where, and when. Keep only details that fit.
“The dog ran.” is a whole sentence, but the reader has questions: What dog? Where did it run? Each detail answers one of those questions before the reader has to ask.

blocks.title: Grow it in steps
blocks.q: “The cat slept.”
steps: What kind of cat? A fluffy cat.
Where? On the warm rug.
When? All afternoon.
Put it together.
blocks.a: “The fluffy cat slept on the warm rug all afternoon.”

blocks.html: Adding details that don’t match, or so many that the sentence runs on and on (“…and it was fun and it was sunny and…”). Add two or three details that help, then stop.

For the grown-up. Play “grow the sentence”: one of you says a short sentence, the other adds one word or phrase, and take turns until it feels just right. If it starts to sound silly, take a detail out.

blocks.html: You know that a sentence starts with a capital letter. There is a word that is always a capital, wherever it is: the word I, when you write about yourself. I is a pronoun.

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: Mom and i baked bread. Then i ate some.
answer: Mom and I baked bread. Then I ate some.
opts.hint: Tap a word to switch its first letter between small and capital. Then Check.

blocks.cap: Fix the word I.

blocks.html: The word I is always a capital letter.

A small i on its own is easy to miss; it can look like part of the next word. Long ago, people copying books by hand began making it tall so it would stand out, printers kept it that way, and we still do.

blocks.title: In the middle of a sentence
blocks.q: “Dad and i went fishing.”
steps: Find the word i. It means the writer.
It is in the middle of the sentence, but it still needs a capital.

blocks.title: Not every i
blocks.q: Does the i in “fishing” need a capital?
steps: That i is a letter inside a word, not the word I.
Only the word I on its own is always a capital.

blocks.html: Writing a small i in the middle of a sentence: “Mom and i baked bread.” After you write, look for every little word i standing alone and make it tall.

For the grown-up. Children often write a capital I at the start of a sentence and a small one in the middle. A quick check after writing (“find every I”) fixes it fast. Letter formation for capital I is in the Handwriting course.

blocks.html: Some nouns are names: the name of one special person or pet. Names begin with a capital letter, just like the word I.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Biscuit is the name of one special dog.
Here grandma is not used as a name. My tells whose grandma.

blocks.cap: Name or not?

blocks.html: Names of people and pets begin with capital letters: Sam, Grandma Rose, Dr. Bell, Biscuit.
A capital letter tells the reader “this is someone’s own name.” There are many dogs, but only one Biscuit. The capital marks the special one.

blocks.title: Two-word names
blocks.q: “We visited aunt rosa.”
steps: Aunt Rosa is the name of one special person.
Each part of the name gets a capital.

blocks.title: Grandma as a name
blocks.q: “Thank you, grandma!” and “I baked with my grandma.”
steps: In the first one, you are talking to her. Grandma is used as her name: Grandma.
In the second, my tells whose grandma. It is not used as a name, so it stays small.
blocks.a: “Thank you, Grandma!” and “I baked with my grandma.”

blocks.html: Capitalizing every noun (Dog, Ball) or forgetting the capital on a pet’s name. Only names get capitals. A quick test: could you put a name like Rosa in its place? Then it is used as a name.
For the grown-up. Titles before a name, like Dr., Mr., Mrs. and Ms., begin with capitals too. Your child’s own name is the first name to get right; check it on every page.

blocks.html: Like names of people, the names of days, months and holidays begin with capital letters. The seasons do not.

head: Capital letter
Small letter
blocks.cap: Days, months and holidays get capitals; seasons don’t.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: Seasons are not names, so they stay small.

blocks.cap: Which words need a capital letter when you write them?

blocks.html: Days, months and holidays begin with capital letters. Seasons do not.
Each day, month and holiday has its own name, like a person does. A season is more like a kind of time of year, so it stays small.

blocks.title: Fix the capitals
blocks.q: “On saturday in june, we had a Summer picnic.”
steps: Saturday is a day: capital.
June is a month: capital.
Summer is a season: small letter.
blocks.a: “On Saturday in June, we had a summer picnic.”

blocks.html: Capitalizing the seasons (Summer, Winter) or forgetting the capital on days and months. Ask: is it a day, a month or a holiday? Capital. A season? Small.
For the grown-up. A calendar on the wall is a ready-made spelling list for the days and months. Writing the date at the top of each page (“Monday, October 6”) practices it every day.

blocks.html: Just like people’s names, the name of one special place begins with capital letters: Oak Street, Lincoln Park, Texas, Chicago, the Pacific Ocean.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: There are many parks. This just tells what kind of place.

blocks.cap: Name or kind of place?

blocks.html: The name of one special place begins with capital letters. A word for a kind of place (park, street, lake) does not.
There are thousands of parks, but only one Lincoln Park in your town. The capitals tell the reader you mean that one place.

blocks.title: Every main word
blocks.q: “We swam in the pacific ocean.”
steps: The Pacific Ocean is the name of one ocean.
Pacific and Ocean are both part of its name, so both get capitals.
The little word the stays small.

blocks.html: Capitalizing any place word: “We went to the Park.” Ask: is it the name of one special place? “Lincoln Park” is; “the park” is not.
For the grown-up. Look at a map together, or at the address on an envelope, and point out the capitals in street, town and state names. Your child’s own address is a great one to learn to write.

blocks.html: Every word has at least one vowel: a, e, i, o or u. In short words like cat, bed, pig, hot and bug, one vowel sits between two other letters and makes its short sound.

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.alt: A cat, a bed, a pig, a dog and the sun

blocks.cap: Short a, short e, short i, short o, short u.

blocks.html: In a short word with one vowel between two consonants, the vowel usually makes its short sound: cat, bed, pig, dog, sun.
Stretch the word out slowly, sound by sound: c-a-t. Each sound gets a letter. Saying it slowly helps you hear the vowel in the middle, so you don’t leave it out.

blocks.title: Pen or pin?
blocks.q: You write with a ___.
steps: Say it slowly: p-e-n.
The middle sound is short e, as in bed.
So it is pen. (A pin is something sharp that holds things.)

blocks.name: wr-sort

opts.readme: Say each word slowly with your child, and listen to the middle sound.

blocks.cap: Short e or short i? Listen closely.

blocks.html: Mixing up short e and short i (pen and pin), or leaving the vowel out (ct for cat). Say the word slowly and touch a finger for each sound; every finger needs a letter.
For the grown-up. Short e and short i sound close in many accents, so this pair takes practice; that is normal. The site’s Phonics Practice has more short-vowel words to read.

blocks.html: Some sounds need two letters working together. These pairs are called digraphs. They come right after short vowel words because they make many short words: ship, chip, thin, when, duck.

head: Letters
At the start
At the end
blocks.cap: Two letters, one sound.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which two letters finish each word?

blocks.html: Two letters can spell one sound: sh, ch, th, wh, and ck at the end of a short word.
English has more sounds than the alphabet has letters. So some letters team up. Ship is not s + hip; the s and h together make one new sound.

blocks.title: Ship or sip?
blocks.q: Spell the word for a big boat.
steps: Say it: ship. The first sound is sh.
One s alone would make sip, a different word.
Use both letters: sh.

blocks.title: Where does ck go?
blocks.q: Spell the bird that says quack.
steps: Say it: d-u-ck.
The last sound comes right after a short vowel at the end of a short word.
That sound is spelled ck.

blocks.html: Writing one letter for the sound (sip for ship, cin for chin), or putting ck at the start of a word. Words start with c or k, never ck.
For the grown-up. Say pairs that differ by the digraph, like sip and ship or cat and chat, and let your child hear the change. The site’s Phonics Practice has a digraph section.

blocks.html: In short vowel words like cap and kit, the vowel makes its short sound. Add an e to the end and listen: cap → cape, kit → kite, hop → hope. The e makes no sound, but the vowel now says its name.

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.alt: A kite, an ice cube and a bone

blocks.cap: Kite, cube, bone: the silent e makes the vowel say its name.

blocks.html: A silent e at the end of a short word makes the vowel say its name: cap → cape, kit → kite, hop → hope.
Without the e, a reader would say kit, not kite. The silent e is a signal: it tells the reader to use the vowel’s long sound, its name.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Read each word aloud. Does the vowel say its name?

blocks.title: Hat or hate?
blocks.q: Spell the thing you wear on your head.
steps: Say it: hat. The a makes its short sound.
No silent e is needed.
Hate, with an e, is a different word.

blocks.html: Leaving the e off (kit when you mean kite), or adding one to a short-vowel word (hate when you mean hat). Say the word: if the vowel says its name, you probably need the e.
For the grown-up. Write a short word on a card and hold a card with a big E next to it: “cap… cape!” Children love the magic of one letter changing the word.

blocks.html: The silent e is one way to spell a long vowel. Another way is a vowel team: two letters together that spell one long sound, like the ai in rain or the ee in tree.

head: Long sound
Teams
Words
blocks.cap: Ay usually comes at the end of a word; ai comes in the middle.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which long sound does each team spell?

blocks.html: Two vowels together often spell one long sound: ai and ay, ee and ea, oa and ow.
English spelling grew over hundreds of years, so one sound can be spelled more than one way. The teams are patterns: once you know them, you can read thousands of words.

blocks.title: Ai or ay?
blocks.q: Spell the word: we like to pl__ outside.
steps: The long a sound comes at the end of the word.
At the end, long a is usually spelled ay.

blocks.title: Ee or ea?
blocks.q: A tree has a green l__f.
steps: Both ee and ea can spell long e.
No rule tells which one; you remember how the word looks.
Leaf uses ea.

blocks.html: Picking the wrong team for a sound (rayn, leef), because several teams spell the same sound. Picture the word as you have seen it in a book. Reading a lot helps you remember which team each word uses.

For the grown-up. When your child is unsure, write the word both ways and ask which one looks right; this builds the visual memory good spellers rely on. Webster’s spelling book, in the site’s teaching guides, groups words by these patterns.

blocks.html: You know that verbs show when, and that most add -ed for the past. Endings like -s, -ed and -ing go on many words. Usually you just add them: jump, jumps, jumped, jumping. Two patterns need care.

head: The word
What to do
Examples
rows: short, one vowel, ends in one consonant (hop, stop)
ends in a silent e (hope, bake)
drop the e before -ing; add just -d for the past
blocks.cap: Endings that start with a vowel are the ones that change things.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: What happens when the ending is added?

blocks.html: Short word, short vowel, one last consonant: double it (hopping). Silent e: drop it before -ing (hoping). Otherwise, just add the ending.
The doubled letter keeps the vowel short. Hoping (one p) says the long o of hope; hopping (two p’s) says the short o of hop. One letter tells the reader which word you mean.

blocks.title: Add -ing to stop
blocks.q: stop + ing
steps: Stop is short, with a short o and one p at the end.
Double the p, then add -ing.

blocks.title: Add -ing to smile
blocks.q: smile + ing
steps: Smile ends in a silent e.
Drop the e, then add -ing.

blocks.html: Forgetting to double (hoping when you mean hopping), or keeping the e (hopeing). Ask: does the word end in a silent e? Is it short, with one vowel and one last consonant?
For the grown-up. Some verbs change in their own way in the past (run, ran), so they skip the -ed rules. A word ending in w, x or y is never doubled: snowing, fixed, played.

blocks.html: Most words follow patterns like vowel teams. But some very common words don’t: said, was, of, they, could, because, friend. If you spell them the way they sound (sed, wuz, uv), they come out wrong. Learn them by heart.

head: Sounds like…
Spelled
blocks.cap: Tricky words, sometimes called heart words: you learn them by heart.

blocks.html: Some common words don’t follow the usual patterns. Learn them by heart, and check them every time you write.
Many of these words are very old, and they kept old spellings while the way we say them changed. Because we use them so often, learning them pays off in every page you write.

blocks.title: Learn a word by heart
blocks.q: friend
steps: Look at it and say each letter: f-r-i-e-n-d.
Notice the tricky part: the i before the e that you can’t hear.
Cover it, write it, then check.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which spellings are right?

blocks.html: Spelling these words the way they sound: sed, wuz, uv, thay, becuz. Sounding out works for most words but not these. Look, say, cover, write, check.
For the grown-up. Keep a short list of your child’s tricky words on the fridge and add one or two a week. The site’s Phonics Practice has a set of heart words.

blocks.html: Short telling sentences are clear, but a page of them can sound choppy: “I have a cat. She is gray.” When two ideas go together, you can join them with and.

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: , and
joins.make: I have a cat, and she is gray.
joins.why: And joins two ideas that go together.

joins.label: , but
joins.make: I have a cat, but she is gray.
joins.why: But is for a surprise or a difference. Nothing here is a surprise.

joins.label: (nothing)
joins.make: I have a cat she is gray.
joins.why: The two ideas run into each other. The reader can’t tell where one stops.

blocks.cap: Tap each way of joining to see the result.

blocks.html: Use and to join two short sentences that go together. Put a comma before and.
Joining two ideas that belong together shows the reader they are connected, and it makes the writing flow like talking.

blocks.title: Join two sentences
blocks.q: “We went to the beach. We built a sandcastle.”
steps: Both ideas are about the same trip.
Keep the first sentence, but change its period to a comma.
Add and, then the second idea with a small letter.
blocks.a: “We went to the beach, and we built a sandcastle.”

blocks.html: Joining every sentence with and, or “and then… and then… and then…”, so the writing becomes one long string. Join two ideas at a time. For a list of events, use separate sentences and time words like first, then and last.

For the grown-up. The comma before and in a joined sentence is the standard way to write it; with two very short sentences, many writers leave it out. And can also join two words: “Mia and Leo,” “cats and dogs.”

blocks.html: You can join two ideas with and when they go together. When the second idea is different, or a surprise, join them with but.

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: , but
joins.make: I like snow, but my dog does not.
joins.why: The two ideas are different, so but fits.

joins.label: , and
joins.make: I like snow, and my dog does not.
joins.why: And is for ideas that go the same way. These two are different.

blocks.cap: And or but? Tap each one.

blocks.html: Use but to join two ideas that are different, or when the second one is a surprise.
But warns the reader: get ready, this next part goes the other way. “The box was big” makes you expect it to be heavy. “…but it was light” surprises you, and but tells you the surprise is coming.

blocks.title: A surprise
blocks.q: “Leo is little. He runs fast.”
steps: You might expect a little boy to be slow.
The second idea is a surprise.
Join them with but.
blocks.a: “Leo is little, but he runs fast.”

blocks.title: No surprise
blocks.q: “I like dogs. I have a dog.”
steps: The two ideas agree. Nothing is a surprise.
So but does not fit. Use and.
blocks.a: “I like dogs, and I have a dog.”

blocks.html: Using but when the two ideas agree: “I like dogs, but I have a dog.” Ask: is the second idea different from what I would expect? If not, use and.
For the grown-up. Some writers and teachers say never to start a sentence with And or But. Careful writers do it often, so it is not an error; for now, practice joining two ideas in one sentence.

blocks.html: Because and so join two ideas when one causes the other. They work like but, but they show why something happened.

head: Reason first, with so
Result first, with because
rows: I was cold, so I put on a coat.
I put on a coat because I was cold.
It started to rain, so we went inside.
We went inside because it started to rain.
blocks.cap: The same two ideas, joined two ways.

blocks.name: wr-combine

joins.label: , so
joins.make: I was hungry, so I ate an apple.
joins.why: So comes right before what happened as a result.

joins.label: because
joins.make: I was hungry because I ate an apple.
joins.why: This says eating the apple made you hungry. The reason and the result are switched.

blocks.cap: Which join makes sense?

blocks.html: Because comes right before the reason. So comes right before the result: what happened.
Readers want to know why. Because and so turn two separate facts into a story of cause and effect, and they make an opinion convincing later on.

blocks.title: Find the reason
blocks.q: “We stayed off the pond ___ the ice was thin.”
steps: Why did we stay off the pond? The ice was thin. That is the reason.
The reason comes right after the blank.
Because goes before the reason.
blocks.a: “We stayed off the pond because the ice was thin.”

blocks.html: Swapping the reason and the result: “I was hungry because I ate lunch.” Ask: which happened first, and which caused the other? The cause goes right after because.

For the grown-up. Ask “why?” about everyday things and let your child answer with because: “Why are you wearing boots?” “Because it is muddy.” Then flip it with so: “It is muddy, so I am wearing boots.”

blocks.html: When you join with and three or more things, you make a list. Commas keep the things in a list apart: “We packed apples, grapes, and cheese.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: We packed apples grapes and cheese
answer: We packed apples, grapes, and cheese.
We packed apples, grapes and cheese.

blocks.cap: Tap the spaces to add commas and a period. Then Check.

blocks.html: Put a comma between the things in a list of three or more.
Without commas, “apples grapes and cheese” runs together, and a reader might stumble. The commas are little pauses that show where each thing ends.

blocks.title: Two ways, both right
blocks.q: Write a list: red, blue, green (my favorite colors).
steps: Put a comma after red and after blue.
Some writers also put one before and: “red, blue, and green.”
Others leave it out: “red, blue and green.” Both ways are used.
blocks.a: “My favorite colors are red, blue, and green.” or “…red, blue and green.”

blocks.title: Only two things
blocks.q: “I like apples and grapes.”
steps: Two things joined by and are not a list of three.
No comma is needed.

blocks.html: Putting a comma after every word (“We, packed, apples…”), or between just two things joined by and. Commas go between the things in a list of three or more.

For the grown-up. The comma before and in a list is called the serial comma. Many book publishers and school style guides use it; most newspapers leave it out. Neither is wrong, so let your child choose one way and use it every time.

blocks.html: When you write about a picture, a good sentence tells three things: who is in it, what they are doing, and where.

blocks.name: wr-picture

opts.sentence: The girl flies a kite at the park.

blocks.cap: Who? The girl. What is she doing? Flying a kite. Where? At the park.

blocks.html: A sentence about a picture tells who, what they are doing, and where.
Your reader can’t see the picture. If you write only “A girl. A kite. A tree.”, they have to guess what is happening. A whole sentence tells them.

blocks.title: Turn a list into a sentence
blocks.q: A picture shows: a dog, a bone, a yard. Someone wrote “A dog. A bone.”
steps: Who? The dog.
What is it doing? Digging for a bone.
Where? In the yard.
Put them together.
blocks.a: “The dog digs for a bone in the yard.”

blocks.name: wr-picture
blocks.cap: Now you: say a sentence with who, what and where. (One way: “The horse eats a carrot on the farm.”)

blocks.html: Listing things in the picture (“A dog. A ball. A tree.”) instead of telling what is happening. Ask the three questions: who? what are they doing? where?

For the grown-up. Picture books are great for this: cover the words, look at a page together, and ask your child to tell you who, what and where in one sentence. Then write it down for them, or let them write it.

blocks.html: A sentence about a picture should tell what the picture really shows: the right who, what and where, and nothing that isn’t there.

blocks.name: wr-picture
blocks.cap: Look closely. Who is here, and where are they?

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: A duck swims on the pond.
A frog sits near the duck.
A duck swims at the beach.
cards.why: The picture shows a pond, not a beach.

cards.text: A duck and a dog swim on the pond.
cards.why: There is no dog in the picture.

blocks.cap: Check each sentence against the picture above.

blocks.html: Choose the sentence that tells what the picture really shows. Check every person, animal, thing and place it names.
Writing about a picture is like being a reporter: readers trust you to tell what is there. A sentence can sound lovely and still be wrong about the picture.

blocks.title: Check every part
blocks.q: The picture shows a boy kicking a ball at the park. Does “The boy kicks the ball at the beach.” match?
steps: Who? The boy: yes.
What? Kicks the ball: yes.
Where? At the beach: no, the picture shows a park.
blocks.a: No. It should say “at the park.”

blocks.html: Picking a sentence that sounds nice but adds something that isn’t in the picture. Go through the sentence word by word and point to each thing in the picture.
For the grown-up. Make it a game: you say a sentence about a picture, sometimes with a mistake in it, and your child catches you. Pointing to each thing named keeps it fair.

blocks.html: When you write a few sentences about a picture or one idea, every sentence should be about that same idea. That is called staying on topic.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Our town park has a new playground.
It has two slides and a rope bridge.

sentences.why: The cousin has nothing to do with the playground.

sentences.text: Kids line up for the swings every afternoon.

blocks.cap: Tap the sentence that does not belong, then Check.

blocks.html: Every sentence should be about the same topic. Take out a sentence that is about something else.
A reader follows your writing like a path. A sentence about something else is a sudden turn: the reader wonders why it is there and loses the way.

blocks.title: Find the stray sentence
blocks.q: “Snow days are fun. We build snowmen. I like pizza. We slide down the hill on sleds.”
steps: What are most of the sentences about? Snow days.
Snowmen and sledding are about snow days.
Pizza is about something else.

blocks.html: Adding a sentence about something else in the middle, just because you thought of it. Read each sentence and ask: is this about my topic? If not, save it for another day.

For the grown-up. Children often add a new thought because it popped into their head; that is how thinking works. You can say, “That’s a good idea for a different page.” Keeping a list of “next time” ideas helps.

blocks.html: Once your sentences stay on topic, you can give them a shape. Start with a sentence that names the topic, give a few facts, and end with a sentence that wraps up.

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: Spiders are good at building webs.
They spin silk thread from their bodies.
They make sticky webs to catch bugs.
A spider’s web is a clever trap.

blocks.cap: The first sentence names the topic; the last one wraps up.

blocks.html: Start with a sentence that tells what your writing is about. Give some facts. End with a sentence that wraps up.
The first sentence is like the title on a box: the reader knows what is inside before opening it. The last sentence tells the reader you are done, so the writing doesn’t just stop.

blocks.title: Write a first sentence
blocks.q: Facts: “It has shelves of picture books. On Tuesdays a librarian reads aloud. You can borrow books for free.” What should come first?
steps: What are all the facts about? The library.
Name that topic in a sentence.
blocks.a: “Our library is a great place to visit.”

blocks.name: wr-para

sentences.text: My grandma has a big garden.
I help her pull the weeds.
Her garden is my favorite place.

blocks.cap: Put the sentences in order: topic first, ending last.

blocks.html: Jumping straight into details without saying what the writing is about, or stopping without an ending sentence. Check: does my first sentence name the topic? Does my last one wrap it up?
For the grown-up. This is the shape of a paragraph, which children will meet again in the Composition course. For now, three or four sentences is plenty.

blocks.html: A friendly letter is writing you send to someone you know. It uses names and dates, and it has five parts, from top to bottom.

blocks.name: wr-note
blocks.cap: Date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

head: Part
What it does
blocks.cap: The five parts of a friendly letter.

blocks.html: A friendly letter has a date, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature, in that order.
A letter is like a visit on paper. You say hello, you talk, you say goodbye, and the person knows who came. The date tells them when.

blocks.title: What is missing?
blocks.q: A letter has a date, “Dear Kai,” a body, and “Your friend,” but no name at the bottom.
steps: Check from top to bottom: date, greeting, body, closing…
After the closing there should be a signature.
Without it, Kai won’t know who wrote the letter.

blocks.name: wr-note
blocks.cap: Put the parts of the letter in order.

blocks.html: Forgetting the greeting or the signature, or writing the closing at the top. Check the five parts in order before you send it.

For the grown-up. Real letters are the best practice. A grandparent, cousin or pen pal who writes back makes letter-writing something children look forward to. The site’s practice sheets print lined paper.

blocks.html: The greeting and the closing are short, but they have their own rules for capitals and commas.

head: Part
Right
Rule
rows: Capital on Dear and on the name; a comma after
Capital on the first word; a comma after
Only the first word gets a capital
blocks.cap: Greetings and closings end with a comma.

blocks.name: wr-note

parts.body: Our class hatched six chicks this week! I named the smallest one Pip.

blocks.cap: Look at the greeting and the closing: capitals and commas.

blocks.html: Start with a greeting like “Dear Grandma,” and end with a closing like “Love,”. Each ends with a comma, and only the first word of the closing gets a capital.
The comma after the greeting is a small pause, like taking a breath after saying hello. Everyone uses the same pattern, so readers spot the start and the end of a letter at a glance.

blocks.title: Fix the closing
blocks.q: “Your Friend”
steps: Only the first word of a closing gets a capital: Your.
Friend stays small.
Add a comma at the end.

blocks.html: Leaving out the comma after the greeting or closing, or capitalizing every word of the closing (“Your Friend,”). Check: capital on the first word, comma at the end.

For the grown-up. In a formal business letter, the greeting traditionally ends with a colon (Dear Ms. Bennett:); children learn that later in Composition. For friendly letters and notes, the comma is standard.

blocks.html: A thank-you note is a short letter that says thanks for a gift or a kindness. A good one does three things.

items: Says thank you and names the gift.
Tells one thing about it: how you used it, or why you like it.
Adds a friendly line for the person, then the closing and your name.

blocks.name: wr-note
blocks.cap: Leo’s thank-you note: thanks, a detail about the kite, and a personal note.

blocks.html: Thank the person, name the gift, say one thing you like about it, and sign your name.
The giver chose the gift with you in mind. When you tell them how you used it, they know it made you happy, and that is the best part of giving.

blocks.title: Make it better
blocks.q: “Thanks for the gift. Bye.”
steps: Which gift? Name it: “Thank you for the purple mittens.”
Say one thing about it: “They kept my hands warm when we went sledding.”
Add a friendly line, a closing and your name.
blocks.a: “Thank you for the purple mittens. They kept my hands warm when we went sledding. I will wear them all winter. Love, Ava”

blocks.html: Writing only “Thanks for the gift.” without naming it or saying anything about it. Every gift is different, so the note should be too.
For the grown-up. After a birthday, write notes a few at a time, not all in one sitting. For a young writer, you can write the greeting and closing and let your child write the two middle sentences.

blocks.html: A story is a set of sentences about one thing that happen in order. Every story has three parts: a beginning, a middle and an end.

blocks.name: wr-picture

frames.caption: Beginning: Mia plants a seed in the yard.
Middle: She waters it every day, and it grows.

blocks.cap: Beginning, middle and end.

head: Part
What it tells
rows: who the story is about, and where
blocks.cap: The three parts of a story.

blocks.html: A story has a beginning (who and where), a middle (what happens) and an end (how it works out).
Readers need to meet the characters before things happen to them, and they want to know how it all turns out. Without an end, a story just stops, and the reader is left hanging.

blocks.title: Which part?
blocks.q: “It was still standing when they went home.”
steps: It does not tell who or where, so it is not the beginning.
It tells how things worked out for the sandcastle.
So it is the end.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: One windy afternoon, Leo took his new kite to the park.
The kite got stuck in a tall tree.
A park worker used a long pole to get it down.
Leo flew his kite again, far away from the trees.
opts.title: Put the story in order

blocks.cap: Tap two sentences to swap them. Then Check.

blocks.html: Stopping in the middle (“…and then I woke up.”) without an ending. Ask: how did it all work out? Write that sentence last.
For the grown-up. When you finish a read-aloud, ask: “How did it start? What happened? How did it end?” Children who can retell a story in three parts are ready to write one.

blocks.html: In a story with a beginning, middle and end, things happen in order. Time words help the reader follow that order: first, next, then, after that, last.

blocks.name: wr-order

items: First, fill a cup with soil.
Next, push a seed into the soil.
Then, water the soil.
Last, set the cup in a sunny window.
opts.title: How to plant a seed

blocks.cap: The time words are clues. Put the steps in order.

blocks.html: Time words like first, next, then and last help a reader follow the order.
A reader can’t ask you “what came next?” Time words answer before they ask. They are signposts on the path through your writing.

blocks.title: Fill in the time words
blocks.q: “___, we got in the car. ___, we drove to the lake. ___, we went swimming.”
steps: The first thing that happened gets First.
A thing in the middle gets Next or Then.
The very last thing gets Last or Finally.
blocks.a: “First, we got in the car. Next, we drove to the lake. Last, we went swimming.”

blocks.html: Using “and then” for every step, or using last before the last step. Save last and finally for the very end, so the reader knows the story is wrapping up.

For the grown-up. Cooking together is a great way to practice: name each step with a time word as you go, then ask your child to tell someone else how you made it. A comma after a time word at the start (First, …) is common; with short words, some writers leave it out.

blocks.html: The beginning of a story tells who and where. Writers have names for these: the characters and the setting.

items: Characters are who the story is about: people or animals.
Setting is where and when the story happens: a place and a time.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: A place is part of the setting, not a character.

cards.text: in a garden behind a barn

blocks.cap: Who, or where and when?

blocks.html: The characters are who the story is about. The setting is where and when it happens.
A reader needs someone to care about and a place to picture. “On a snowy night in the woods, a little fox…” gives both in one sentence, and the story can begin.

blocks.title: Find them
blocks.q: “One windy afternoon, Leo took his new kite to the park.”
steps: Who? Leo: a character.
Where? At the park: the setting.
When? One windy afternoon: also the setting.
blocks.a: Character: Leo. Setting: the park, on a windy afternoon.

blocks.html: Calling the place a character, or forgetting to tell where and when the story happens. Characters do things; the setting is where and when they do them.
For the grown-up. A pet or a toy can be a character if the story is about it. When your child starts a story, ask: “Who is it about? Where are they? When is it?”

blocks.html: Many stories have a problem in the middle: something goes wrong for the characters. Then, near the end, they find a fix, called the solution.

blocks.name: wr-picture

frames.caption: Problem: the kite is stuck in a tree.
Fix: a park worker gets it down, and Leo flies it again.

blocks.cap: A problem in the middle, and a fix at the end.

blocks.html: Many stories have a problem in the middle and a fix at the end.
A problem makes the reader wonder, “What will they do?” That wondering keeps them reading. If the problem is fixed right away, there is nothing to wonder about.

blocks.title: Find the problem and the fix
blocks.q: “Nora and her mom baked a cake. There was no sugar left. Their neighbor lent them a cup. Grandpa loved the cake.”
steps: What goes wrong? There was no sugar left. That is the problem.
What do they do about it? The neighbor lends them sugar. That is the fix.
blocks.a: Problem: no sugar. Fix: the neighbor lends a cup.

blocks.html: Solving the problem right away, so the story has no middle. Let the characters try something, or wait a little, before the fix comes.
For the grown-up. Ask about favorite books: “What was the problem? How did they fix it?” Then help your child plan a story by choosing a problem first.

blocks.html: How-to writing tells a reader how to do something, step by step, using time words. The test: could someone who has never done it follow your steps?

blocks.name: wr-order

items: Get two slices of bread.
Spread jam on one slice.
Put the other slice on top.
Cut the sandwich in half.
opts.title: How to make a jam sandwich

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order. Which one must come first?

blocks.html: Tell how to do something with every step, in order, so a reader could follow it.
You know how to do it, so some steps seem too easy to write. But the reader only knows what you tell them. A skipped step leaves them stuck.

blocks.title: Find the missing step
blocks.q: “1. Fill a cup with soil. 2. Water the soil. 3. Set the cup in a sunny window.”
steps: Pretend you have never planted a seed. Follow the steps.
You have soil and water, but where is the seed?
A step is missing between 1 and 2.
blocks.a: Add “Push a seed into the soil.” after step 1.

blocks.html: Skipping steps that seem obvious, like getting the bread out before spreading the jam. Act it out while someone reads your steps aloud: do only what the words say.
For the grown-up. A funny way to test how-to writing: follow your child’s steps exactly as written. If the bread never comes out of the bag, they will see the missing step for themselves.

blocks.html: An opinion tells what you think or feel: “I think dogs are the best pets.” A good opinion gives a reason, often with because: “…because they love to play.”
A fact is different: it can be checked. “Dogs have four legs.” is a fact. Other people may not share your opinion, and that’s fine.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: Saturday is the best day of the week.

cards.why: Some people like pears better. It is what someone thinks.

cards.text: I think cats make great pets.

blocks.cap: Can it be checked, or is it what someone thinks?

blocks.html: An opinion says what you think and gives a reason: “I think…, because….”
A reason helps your reader understand you. They may still disagree, but they know why you think so, and that is how people share ideas.

blocks.title: Add a reason
blocks.q: “I think summer is the best season.”
steps: That is the opinion.
Why? Ask yourself what you love about summer.
Add because and the reason.
blocks.a: “I think summer is the best season because we can swim every day.”

blocks.html: Giving an opinion with no reason, or giving a fact (“Dogs have four legs.”) when you were asked for an opinion. Check: does it say what I think? Does it say why?

For the grown-up. Opinion writing at this age is about favorites: foods, seasons, books, games. Ask your child for a reason and then a second one; this grows into persuasive writing in the Composition course.

blocks.html: Good writers read their writing back before they say “done.” Use everything you’ve learned: capital letters, end marks, names and tricky words.

blocks.name: wr-checklist
blocks.cap: Tap each item as you check it. You can print this list.

blocks.html: Read your writing back, aloud if you can. Check capitals, spaces, end marks and spelling.
When you write, your mind is busy with ideas. When you read it back, you see what is really on the page. Reading aloud helps most: your ear catches what your eye misses.

blocks.title: Check a sentence
blocks.q: “today Leo and I ate lunch outside”
steps: Start: today needs a capital: Today.
Names and I: Leo and I are fine.
End: it tells something, so it needs a period.
blocks.a: “Today Leo and I ate lunch outside.”

blocks.name: wr-punct

opts.text: we fed the ducks at the pond they were hungry
answer: We fed the ducks at the pond. They were hungry.

blocks.cap: Fix the capitals and end marks, then Check.

blocks.html: Saying “I’m done” without reading the writing back. Reading it aloud, slowly, catches most mistakes.
For the grown-up. Let your child be the one to find the mistakes. Instead of pointing to them, you can say “I see two things to fix in this line” and let them hunt.

blocks.html: When you check your writing, a sentence can have more than one mistake. Fixing one and stopping is the trap. Check every part, every time.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments.why: A sentence starts with a capital letter.
Maya is a name, so it needs a capital.
The word I is always a capital.
The past of go is went.
A telling sentence ends with a period.

blocks.cap: Tap Next to make one fix at a time.

blocks.html: A sentence can have more than one mistake. Check the start, names and I, each word, and the end.
Mistakes like to hide together. If you stop at the first one, the reader still trips on the others. A checking order makes sure nothing gets skipped.

blocks.title: Check in order
blocks.q: “we was happy when aunt rosa came”
steps: The start: we → We.
Names and I: aunt rosa → Aunt Rosa.
Each word: was → were (more than one, in writing).
The end: add a period.
blocks.a: “We were happy when Aunt Rosa came.”

blocks.html: Fixing one mistake and stopping. After each fix, keep going through the checklist: start, names and I, each word, end.

For the grown-up. A fixed order (start, names and I, words, end) turns editing into a routine children can do on their own. Praise the fixes they find, not only the clean copy. “We was” is common in everyday speech; the fix here is about written standard English.
